docs.title: A. Numerical Features
docs.text:
The table below describes the three numerical features over all 30,000 employees, and Figure 1 shows a histogram and a boxplot for each. Histograms were chosen to show shape, modes and skewness, and boxplots to show quartiles, spread and outliers under the IQR rule (values outside \([Q_1 - 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR},\ Q_3 + 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}]\)).

   import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
   import seaborn as sns

   numeric_cols = ["tenure_years", "performance_rating", "salary_k_usd"]

   # Descriptive statistics
   summary = df[numeric_cols].describe().T.rename(columns={
       "count": "Count",
       "mean": "Mean",
       "std": "Std. deviation",
       "min": "Minimum",
       "25%": "Q1",
       "50%": "Median",
       "75%": "Q3",
       "max": "Maximum",
   })

   summary["Missing"] = df[numeric_cols].isna().sum()
   summary["Skewness"] = df[numeric_cols].skew()

   # IQR rule: values outside [Q1 - 1.5 × IQR, Q3 + 1.5 × IQR]
   summary["IQR"] = summary["Q3"] - summary["Q1"]
   summary["IQR outliers"] = [
       (
           (df[col] < summary.loc[col, "Q1"] - 1.5 * summary.loc[col, "IQR"])
           | (df[col] > summary.loc[col, "Q3"] + 1.5 * summary.loc[col, "IQR"])
       ).sum()
       for col in numeric_cols
   ]

   display(summary.round(2))

Descriptive statistics of the numerical features.

Feature Count Mean Std. dev. Min Q1 Median Q3 Max Skewness IQR IQR outliers tenure_years 30,000 4.38 3.10 0.1 2.1 3.7 5.9 25.0 1.43 3.8 950 performance_rating 30,000 3.39 0.87 1.0 2.8 3.4 4.0 5.0 −0.16 1.2 0 salary_k_usd 30,000 163.65 66.22 51 114 151 198 600 1.06 84 806 
   units = {
       "tenure_years": "Years",
       "performance_rating": "Rating (1–5)",
       "salary_k_usd": "Thousands of USD per year",
   }

   fig, axes = plt.subplots(
       nrows=len(numeric_cols),
       ncols=2,
       figsize=(13, 4 * len(numeric_cols)),
       constrained_layout=True,
   )

   for row, col in enumerate(numeric_cols):
       values = df[col].dropna()

       # Histogram: distribution shape and possible peaks
       sns.histplot(values, bins="auto", ax=axes[row, 0], color="#4277a5")
       axes[row, 0].axvline(
           values.mean(), color="darkred", linestyle="--", label="Mean"
       )
       axes[row, 0].axvline(
           values.median(), color="black", linestyle=":", label="Median"
       )
       axes[row, 0].set(
           title=f"{col} — Distribution",
           xlabel=units[col],
           ylabel="Number of employees",
       )
       axes[row, 0].legend()

       # Boxplot: quartiles, spread and potential outliers
       sns.boxplot(x=values, ax=axes[row, 1], color="#91b7d5")
       axes[row, 1].set(
           title=f"{col} — Boxplot",
           xlabel=units[col],
       )

   plt.savefig("./figures/figure1.png", dpi=150)
   plt.show()

Figure 1. Histograms (left, with mean and median) and boxplots (right) of tenure_years, performance_rating and salary_k_usd.

Tenure. tenure_years is concentrated at shorter durations, with a single broad peak around 2–3 years and a long right tail. Its mean (4.38 years) exceeds its median (3.7 years), consistent with positive skewness (1.43). The IQR rule flags 950 employees (3.17%) with tenure above 11.6 years. These values extend up to 25 years but are plausible employment durations.

Performance rating. performance_rating is broadly centered around 3.4, with a mean of 3.39 and a median of 3.4. Its skewness of −0.16 indicates only a slight left skew. The histogram has one broad central peak and a noticeable concentration at the maximum rating of 5.0. No values fall outside the 1–5 scale, and none are flagged by the IQR rule.

Salary. salary_k_usd has a broad peak around USD 100,000–150,000 per year and a long right tail. Its mean (USD 163,650) exceeds its median (USD 151,000), consistent with positive skewness (1.06). The IQR rule flags 806 employees (2.69%) with salaries above USD 324,000. The maximum is USD 600,000, which is high but plausible for the most senior level (Stage 3C shows a median of USD 300,000 for lead).

Conclusion (Figure 1): tenure and salary are right-skewed with plausible long tails, while performance rating is close to symmetric. Skewed features and different scales motivate the scaling decision in Stage 4.

Spearman's rank correlation was used because tenure and salary are right-skewed with high values, and because the analysis should not assume that any relationship is linear. It was computed on the development set only.

   # Correlation matrix: development data only
   corr = X_dev[numeric_cols].corr(method="spearman")

   plt.figure(figsize=(6, 5))
   sns.heatmap(
       corr,
       annot=True,
       fmt=".2f",
       cmap="coolwarm",

   plt.tight_layout()

Figure 2. Spearman correlation matrix of the numerical features (development set).

Figure 3. Scatter plots for each pair of numerical features (random sample of 5,000 development employees).

All three correlations are close to zero: tenure and performance rating (ρ = 0.007), tenure and salary (ρ = 0.007), and performance rating and salary (ρ = −0.006). The scatter plots show no increasing or decreasing pattern.

Conclusion (Figures 2 and 3): no strong monotonic relationship and no redundant pair exists among the numerical predictors, so none needs to be removed. Correlations near zero do not rule out more complex, non-monotonic relationships.

For every categorical feature, Figure 4 shows the proportion of employees laid off within each category of the development set, against the overall rate of 20.36%.

   categorical_cols = [
       "department",
       "cost_center_type",

       "level",
       "team_wind_down",
       "is_recent_hire",

   ]

   binary_cols = {
       "team_wind_down",
       "is_recent_hire",

   # Rejoin predictors and target by their original row indices for analysis.

           )
           .reset_index()
           .rename(columns={col: "category"})

       ].sort_values("laid_off_pct", ascending=False)

       ax.set_xlabel("Laid off within category (%)")
       ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
       ax.legend(fontsize=8)

   for ax in list(axes.flat)[len(categorical_cols):]:
       ax.set_visible(False)

   plt.savefig("./figures/figure4.png", dpi=150)
   plt.show()

Figure 4. Percentage of employees laid off within each category, for each categorical feature (development set). The dashed line marks the overall rate (20.4%).

The largest difference appears for team_wind_down: about 73% of employees whose teams were being eliminated were laid off, compared with about 12% of the others. Employees in cost centers (about 37%) were laid off far more often than those in revenue-generating areas (about 12%). Employees on a performance improvement plan and those in redundant roles also had higher rates than their comparison groups. Across departments, recruiting, research, and general and administrative roles had the highest rates (35–39%), while engineering, product, data and sales had the lowest (about 12–13%). Recent hires had a higher rate than other employees. Differences by management layer and seniority level were smaller, and remote and non-remote employees had nearly identical rates (20.28% and 20.42%).

Conclusion (Figure 4): the structural features team_wind_down, cost_center_type and role_redundant, together with department and on_pip, are the most strongly associated with layoffs, while remote carries almost no signal. These are descriptive associations, not causal evidence.

Figure 5a. tenure_years across the groups of each categorical feature (development set).

Tenure. Medians (3.6–3.9 years) and IQRs (3.6–4.0 years) are similar in almost every group. The clear exception is is_recent_hire: recent hires have a median tenure of 0.6 years and an IQR of 0.4, against 3.9 years and 3.7 for the others, as expected from the definition of the feature.

Conclusion (Figure 5a): tenure differs only for the feature derived from it, so the categorical variables carry no additional information about tenure.

Figure 5b. performance_rating across the groups of each categorical feature (development set).

Performance rating. Employees on a performance improvement plan (on_pip = 1) differ in both location and spread: their median rating is 2.1, against 3.5 for the others, and their IQR is 0.5, against 1.2. All other groups have median 3.4–3.5 and IQR 1.2–1.3.

Conclusion (Figure 5b): only on_pip separates performance ratings, in location and in spread; the plan is closely tied to low ratings.

Figure 5c. salary_k_usd across the groups of each categorical feature (development set).

Salary. Seniority level shows the clearest difference. Median salary rises from USD 95,000 (junior) to 140,000 (mid), 185,000 (senior), 252,000 (staff) and 300,000 (lead), and the spread widens with level (IQR of 23, 34, 45, 60 and 71 thousand USD). Employees with high_salary = 1 have a median of 243 against 133 thousand USD (IQR 69 against 57), which is expected from the definition. In the remaining groups, medians stay at 148–154 and IQRs at 80–89 thousand USD.

Conclusion (Figure 5c): salary depends on seniority in both location and spread, so level and salary_k_usd carry overlapping information even though the numerical features are uncorrelated with each other.

Overall, the most pronounced group differences are tied to features that directly describe or are derived from the numerical variable being plotted.

docs.title: A. Strategies
docs.text:
Each strategy described in the table below is tied to the finding that motivates it.

Step Finding Strategy Missing values The three numerical features and all categorical features had no missing values. Keep a median imputer for numerical features, a most-frequent imputer for binary features, and an explicit "Missing" category for text features as safeguards for future inputs. Fit them on the training folds only. Outliers The IQR rule flagged 950 tenure values and 806 salary values, but their ranges (up to 25 years and USD 600,000) are plausible and consistent with seniority (Figure 5c). Keep these records: 0 rows are removed or modified. An IQR flag alone is not evidence of an error. Standardization limits their influence on training. Categorical encoding The four text predictors have low cardinality (3 to 9), and level has named categories with no demonstrated equal spacing between them. One-hot encode the four text predictors. Leave the six binary predictors as 0/1. Category absent from training A category may appear in a validation fold or the test set that was absent from training. Use handle_unknown="ignore": the encoder keeps the columns learned during training and represents the unseen category with zeros in that feature's encoded columns, so the number and order of columns do not change (scikit-learn OneHotEncoder). Scaling Tenure (0.1–25), rating (1–5) and salary (51–600 thousand USD) are on different scales; salary is stored in thousands of USD, not in USD. Standardize the three continuous features so their scales are comparable for neural network training. Keep binary and one-hot features at 0/1.

The pipeline is fitted on training data only: inside each cross-validation iteration it is fitted on the four training folds and applied to the held-out fold, and for the final model it is fitted on the full development set and applied to the test set. The code below fits the preprocessor on the development set and checks the pipeline under 5-fold cross-validation for each feature set.

   from preprocessing import (
       ALL_FEATURE_COLUMNS, FEATURE_SETS, fit_transform_dev_test, iter_cv_folds,
   )

   # Exploration (PCA / t-SNE / UMAP below): all 13 features, fitted on the
   # development set only. The target is never used.
   preprocessor, X_dev_ready, X_test_ready = fit_transform_dev_test(
       X_dev, X_test, ALL_FEATURE_COLUMNS
   )

   # Check the leakage-safe pipeline under 5-fold CV for each feature set.
   # The pipeline is re-fitted inside every iteration on the 4 training folds.
   cv_rows = []
   for set_name, columns in FEATURE_SETS.items():
       for fold in iter_cv_folds(X_dev, y_dev, columns, n_splits=N_SPLITS):
           cv_rows.append({
               "Feature set": set_name,
               "Fold": fold.number,
               "Train shape": fold.X_train.shape,
               "Validation shape": fold.X_val.shape,
               "Train laid off (%)": round(fold.y_train.mean() * 100, 2),
               "Validation laid off (%)": round(fold.y_val.mean() * 100, 2),
               "NaN values": int(
                   np.isnan(fold.X_train).sum() + np.isnan(fold.X_val).sum()
               ),
           })

   display(pd.DataFrame(cv_rows))

   for set_name, columns in FEATURE_SETS.items():
       _, dev_arr, test_arr = fit_transform_dev_test(
           X_dev, X_test, columns, verbose=False
       )
       print(f"{set_name}: development {dev_arr.shape}, test {test_arr.shape}")
       print("  features:", list(
           iter_cv_folds(X_dev, y_dev, columns).__next__()
           .pipeline.get_feature_names_out()
       ))

In all 10 runs (2 feature sets × 5 folds) the training matrices have shape (19200, 24) for baseline and (19200, 29) for extended, the validation matrices have 4,800 rows, and 0 NaN values remain. The layoff proportion stays at 20.35–20.36% in every training fold.

   from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

   feature_names = preprocessor.get_feature_names_out()

   pca = PCA(svd_solver="full")
   pca.fit(X_dev_ready)  # Full development set; no validation or test data

   cumulative_variance = np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)

   fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))

   print(f"PC1 variance: {pca.explained_variance_ratio_[0]:.1%}")
   print(f"PC2 variance: {pca.explained_variance_ratio_[1]:.1%}")
   print(f"First two PCs combined: {cumulative_variance[1]:.1%}")

   for threshold in (0.80, 0.90):
       n_components = np.searchsorted(cumulative_variance, threshold) + 1
       print(f"Components needed for {threshold:.0%} variance: {n_components}")

   # Largest positive and negative coefficients for the first two components.
   loadings = pd.DataFrame(
       pca.components_[:2].T,
       index=feature_names,
       columns=["PC1", "PC2"],
   )

       print(f"\nLargest absolute {component} coefficients:")

           loadings[[component]]
           .assign(abs_coefficient=lambda t: t[component].abs())
           .sort_values("abs_coefficient", ascending=False)
           .head(10)
           .drop(columns="abs_coefficient")
           .round(3)
       )

Figure 6. Cumulative explained variance of the principal components (development set). Dashed lines mark 80% and 90%.

PC1 explains 19.8% of the variance and PC2 explains 16.1%, so the first two components together explain 35.8%. Around 9 components are needed to retain 80% and 14 to retain 90%. The variance is therefore spread over many components, and a 2D projection keeps only about a third of the information.

The table below shows th largest absolute loadings of the first two principal components.

PC1 Loading PC2 Loading salary_k_usd 0.887 performance_rating 0.851 high_salary 0.329 tenure_years 0.512 level_junior −0.226 on_pip −0.105 level_staff 0.127 is_recent_hire −0.045 level_mid −0.114 remote 0.012

PC2 is driven mainly by performance rating and tenure, with a smaller negative contribution from on_pip, so it represents a performance and tenure direction. These loadings describe directions of variation in the inputs; they do not measure association with the target.

t-SNE and UMAP. To keep the computation tractable, t-SNE and UMAP were applied to a stratified sample of 5,000 development employees (layoff rate 20.4%), using two values of perplexity (30 and 100) for t-SNE and two values of n_neighbors (15 and 50) for UMAP. The PCA projection of the same sample is shown for comparison.

   import umap

   y_dev_array = np.asarray(y_dev)

   sample_size = min(5_000, len(y_dev_array))
   all_indices = np.arange(len(y_dev_array))

           all_indices,

   projections = {

   iteration_arg = (
       "max_iter" if "max_iter" in inspect.signature(TSNE).parameters
       else "n_iter"
   )

       model = TSNE(
           n_components=2,
           perplexity=perplexity,
           init="pca",
           learning_rate="auto",
           random_state=42,
           **{iteration_arg: 1000},
       )
       projections[f"t-SNE (perplexity={perplexity})"] = (
           model.fit_transform(X_sample)
       )

   for n_neighbors in (15, 50):
       model = umap.UMAP(
           n_components=2,
           n_neighbors=n_neighbors,
           min_dist=0.1,
           random_state=42,
       )
       projections[f"UMAP (n_neighbors={n_neighbors})"] = (
           model.fit_transform(X_sample)
       )

   fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(18, 11), constrained_layout=True)

   for ax, (title, coordinates) in zip(axes.flat, projections.items()):
       for cls, label, color in [
           (0, "Retained (0)", "#4277a5"),
           (1, "Laid off (1)", "#dc6949"),
       ]:
           mask = y_sample == cls
           ax.scatter(
               coordinates[mask, 0],
               coordinates[mask, 1],
               s=8,
               alpha=0.45,
               c=color,
               label=label,
               rasterized=True,
           )

       ax.set_title(title)
       ax.set_xlabel("Component 1" if title == "PCA" else "Embedding 1")
       ax.set_ylabel("Component 2" if title == "PCA" else "Embedding 2")

   for ax in list(axes.flat)[len(projections):]:
       ax.set_visible(False)

   axes.flat[0].legend(markerscale=2)
   plt.savefig("./figures/figure7.png", dpi=150)
   plt.show()

Figure 7. Two-dimensional projections of the preprocessed development sample, colored by laid_off: PCA, t-SNE (perplexity 30 and 100) and UMAP (n_neighbors 15 and 50).

Comparison. In the PCA projection, retained and laid-off employees overlap substantially. t-SNE and UMAP reveal several local groups that are less apparent in PCA, but both classes appear within most groups. The groups also change in shape and arrangement across the two perplexity values and the two n_neighbors values, so they should not be over-interpreted. Cluster sizes and inter-cluster distances in t-SNE and UMAP have no direct interpretation in the original feature space.

Conclusion (Figure 7): the nonlinear projections reveal local feature structure that PCA does not, but none of the three methods shows a clear separation between laid-off and retained employees. Class separability cannot be judged from these plots and must be established on held-out data.

docs.title: C. Pipeline
docs.text:
The preprocessing pipeline lives in code/preprocessing.py and is parameterized by feature set. It can be imported with:

from preprocessing import FEATURE_SETS, fit_transform_dev_test, iter_cv_folds

A ColumnTransformer within a Pipeline applies:

  • median imputation and standardization to the numerical features;
  • explicit missing-category imputation and one-hot encoding (handle_unknown="ignore") to the text categories;
  • most-frequent imputation to the binary features.

It is fitted on training data only: inside each cross-validation iteration on the four training folds (19,200 employees) and then applied, without refitting, to the validation fold (4,800 employees); for the final model, on the full development set (24,000 employees) and then applied, without refitting, to the test set (6,000 employees). The target laid_off and the identifier employee_id are excluded from the input features.

No NaN values remain in any split (0 in the development and test sets, and in every fold). Table 12 gives the output shapes.

The table below shows the output shape after the pipeline.

Feature set Columns Per-fold train Per-fold validation Development Test baseline 24 (19200, 24) (4800, 24) (24000, 24) (6000, 24) extended 29 (19200, 29) (4800, 29) (24000, 29) (6000, 29)

Feature names (extended, 29 columns).

  • numerical (3): tenure_years, performance_rating, salary_k_usd
  • department (9): data, engineering, g_and_a, marketing, product, recruiting, research, sales, support
  • cost_center_type (3): cost_center, revenue, support
  • mgmt_layer (3): IC, director, manager
  • level (5): junior, lead, mid, senior, staff
  • binary (6): team_wind_down, is_recent_hire, on_pip, high_salary, remote, role_redundant

The baseline set (24 columns) is the same list without the 5 columns of the structural drivers: the 3 cost_center_type columns, team_wind_down and role_redundant. In the code, the names carry the prefixes numeric__, categorical__ and binary__.

   from typing import Iterator, NamedTuple, Optional, Sequence

   import numpy as np
   from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
   from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
   from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold
   from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
   from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler


   NUMERIC_COLUMNS = ["tenure_years", "performance_rating", "salary_k_usd"]
   CATEGORICAL_COLUMNS = [
       "department", "cost_center_type", "mgmt_layer", "level",
   ]
   BINARY_COLUMNS = [
       "team_wind_down", "is_recent_hire", "on_pip",
       "high_salary", "remote", "role_redundant",
   ]
   ALL_FEATURE_COLUMNS = NUMERIC_COLUMNS + CATEGORICAL_COLUMNS + BINARY_COLUMNS
   FEATURE_COLUMNS = ALL_FEATURE_COLUMNS

   # Feature sets suggested by the dataset author ("Modeling note").
   # Both sets share every remaining predictor (salary_k_usd, department,
   # mgmt_layer, level, is_recent_hire, high_salary, remote, ...); they differ
   # only in the three structural drivers.
   #   baseline : all predictors EXCEPT the structural drivers (performance_rating,
   #              tenure_years and on_pip are included) -> expected to barely beat chance.
   #   extended : baseline + team_wind_down, cost_center_type, role_redundant
   #              -> expected strong.
   STRUCTURAL_FEATURES = ["team_wind_down", "cost_center_type", "role_redundant"]
   BASELINE_FEATURES = [c for c in ALL_FEATURE_COLUMNS if c not in STRUCTURAL_FEATURES]
   FEATURE_SETS = {
       "baseline": BASELINE_FEATURES,
       "extended": BASELINE_FEATURES + STRUCTURAL_FEATURES,
   }

   RANDOM_STATE = 42
   N_SPLITS = 5


   def _check_columns(frame, feature_columns, name):
       missing = sorted(set(feature_columns) - set(frame.columns))
       if missing:
           raise ValueError(f"{name} is missing feature columns: {missing}")
       forbidden = sorted({"employee_id", "laid_off"} & set(frame.columns))
       if forbidden:
           raise ValueError(
               f"{name} contains {forbidden}; separate the target and "
               "remove the identifier before preprocessing."
           )


   def make_preprocessing_pipeline(feature_columns: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None):
       """Build an unfitted pipeline for dense neural-network inputs.

       ``feature_columns`` selects which columns enter the model (default: all 13).
       Each column is routed to the numeric / categorical / binary branch it
       belongs to; branches left empty by the selection are omitted.
       """
       selected = list(ALL_FEATURE_COLUMNS if feature_columns is None else feature_columns)
       unknown = sorted(set(selected) - set(ALL_FEATURE_COLUMNS))
       if unknown:
           raise ValueError(f"Unknown feature columns: {unknown}")

       numeric_cols = [c for c in NUMERIC_COLUMNS if c in selected]
       categorical_cols = [c for c in CATEGORICAL_COLUMNS if c in selected]
       binary_cols = [c for c in BINARY_COLUMNS if c in selected]

       transformers = []
       if numeric_cols:
           transformers.append(("numeric", Pipeline([
               ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
               ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
           ]), numeric_cols))
       if categorical_cols:
           transformers.append(("categorical", Pipeline([
               ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="Missing")),
               ("encoder", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False)),
           ]), categorical_cols))
       if binary_cols:
           transformers.append(("binary", Pipeline([
               ("imputer", SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent")),
           ]), binary_cols))

       columns = ColumnTransformer(transformers=transformers, remainder="drop")
       return Pipeline([("features", columns)])


   def _fit_transform(X_fit, X_others, feature_columns):
       """Fit on ``X_fit`` only; transform it and every frame in ``X_others``."""
       pipeline = make_preprocessing_pipeline(feature_columns)
       fitted = np.asarray(pipeline.fit_transform(X_fit[list(feature_columns)]),
                           dtype=np.float32)
       others = [
           np.asarray(pipeline.transform(X[list(feature_columns)]), dtype=np.float32)
           for X in X_others
       ]
       for values in [fitted, *others]:
           if not np.isfinite(values).all():
               raise ValueError("Array contains NaN or infinite values after preprocessing")
       return pipeline, fitted, others


   class Fold(NamedTuple):
       """One cross-validation iteration, already preprocessed."""
       number: int            # 1-based
       pipeline: Pipeline     # fitted on this fold's training part only
       X_train: np.ndarray
       X_val: np.ndarray
       y_train: np.ndarray
       y_val: np.ndarray


   def iter_cv_folds(X_dev, y_dev, feature_columns: Sequence[str],
                     n_splits: int = N_SPLITS,
                     random_state: int = RANDOM_STATE) -> Iterator[Fold]:
       """Yield stratified K-fold iterations over the development set.

       The preprocessing pipeline is fitted on the training part of each fold
       (K-1 folds) and applied to the held-out fold, so no statistics of the
       validation fold (means, medians, categories) leak into training.
       """
       _check_columns(X_dev, feature_columns, "Development set")
       y_array = np.asarray(y_dev)
       skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=random_state)

       for number, (train_idx, val_idx) in enumerate(skf.split(X_dev, y_array), start=1):
           pipeline, X_tr, (X_va,) = _fit_transform(
               X_dev.iloc[train_idx], [X_dev.iloc[val_idx]], feature_columns
           )
           yield Fold(number, pipeline, X_tr, X_va, y_array[train_idx], y_array[val_idx])


   def fit_transform_dev_test(X_dev, X_test, feature_columns: Sequence[str],
                              verbose: bool = True):
       """Fit on the whole development set (80%); transform the untouched test set.

       Use for the final model after cross-validation has chosen hyper-parameters.
       Returns ``(pipeline, dev_array, test_array)`` as ``float32`` arrays.
       """
       _check_columns(X_dev, feature_columns, "Development set")
       _check_columns(X_test, feature_columns, "Test set")
       pipeline, dev, (test,) = _fit_transform(X_dev, [X_test], feature_columns)

       if verbose:
           names = pipeline.get_feature_names_out()
           print(f"Development: shape={dev.shape}, NaN values={int(np.isnan(dev).sum())}")
           print(f"Test:        shape={test.shape}, NaN values={int(np.isnan(test).sum())}")
           print(f"Final feature count: {len(names)}")
           for feature in names:
               print(f"  {feature}")
       return pipeline, dev, test

docs.title: Main Findings
docs.text:
1. The target is imbalanced. 6,107 employees (20.36%) were laid off, against 23,893 retained, a ratio of 3.91:1 (Table 4). The stratified split keeps this proportion in the development set, test set and every fold.
  2. Structural features are the strongest signals. Layoff rates are 73.28% when team_wind_down = 1 against 11.57% otherwise, and 37.26% in cost centers against 12.30% in revenue areas (Figure 4, Table 9). Department, on_pip (37.26% against 19.03%) and role_redundant (32.12% against 18.74%) also differ clearly, while remote shows no difference (Figure 4).
  3. The numerical predictors are not redundant with each other, with all pairwise |ρ| ≤ 0.007. They are, however, tied to derived features: is_recent_hire follows from tenure, and salary follows seniority.
  4. The data are clean. There are no missing or invalid values, and the outliers flagged by the IQR rule are plausible.
  5. The classes are not visibly separable in 2D. PC1 + PC2 explain 35.8% of the variance (Figure 6), and PCA, t-SNE and UMAP show overlapping classes (Figure 7).

docs.title: Risks and Handling Plan
docs.text:
The table below shows the risks for modeling and how to handle them.

Risk Handling plan Class imbalance (3.91:1) makes accuracy misleading. Use stratified splits (already in place), metrics such as precision, recall, F1 and PR-AUC rather than accuracy alone, class weights, and a decision threshold chosen on the cross-validation folds, never on the test set. A single dominant feature: team_wind_down has by far the largest difference in layoff rate (Figure 4) and could overshadow the other features. Compare feature sets and check permutation importance; interpret the baseline model separately. Weak separability of individual attributes in 2D (Figure 7). Do not draw conclusions from the projections; rely on cross-validated performance and consider nonlinear interactions between features. Redundancy by construction: is_recent_hire and high_salary are derived from continuous features, and level is tied to salary. Keep them (the redundancy is deterministic), use regularization, and check whether removing them changes validation performance. Unseen categories in validation or test data. handle_unknown="ignore" in the encoder keeps the input dimension fixed. Synthetic data: the structure may be simpler than a real layoff. Treat results as a property of this dataset; do not use the model to make decisions about real employees.
